opening.headline: To determine whether data containing customer information can be entered into AI, you need to know the type of information and the criteria for judging before inputting it.
body: There are times when you want to quickly summarize a file containing customer names, contact information, and purchase history by uploading it to AI. If you don't have a standard to determine whether it's okay to raise something, you end up making a decision based on your intuition every time, and a single mistake can have an impact on both the customer and the organization.

In this class, you will distinguish between personal information and confidential information, and read what each service's usage policy and conduct principles document says. Check the Gemini API documentation to see how the service handles the entered data. At the end, we create a form that can be entered as an example summarizing customer consultation records.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the types of personal and confidential information and input judgment criteria
You can determine whether data can be entered or not.

screens.title: Can I include data containing customer information?
screens.lead: This is a scene we often encounter at work. Please read the information below and consider whether you can upload this data to AI as is.

visual.alt: A scene with a customer list spreadsheet model on the left, an AI input window on the right, and a question mark between the two.

paragraphs: I have a file with customer names, contact information, and purchase details. I want to quickly summarize the consultation and upload it to AI. Just upload your file and it'll be done in a matter of minutes.

The problem is when there is no standard to determine whether it is okay to upload something. Without a standard, you end up deciding based on how you feel that day or how busy you are. Some days I'm careful, and some days I just post it. Because it is difficult to undo information once entered, judgment must be made before entering.

The goal of this class is to have standards for making your own judgments before entering anything. First, we start by dividing information into personal information, confidential information, and general information.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is it safe to enter if I just delete the name and contact information column from the customer list? You will be able to answer this question at the end of the lesson.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed that standards are needed, let's start by recalling the standards I have.

screens.title: Standards for data that should not be entered
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What do you think are the standards for data that should not be entered?
items.answer: If you can think of something like your name, customer information, or plans you haven't revealed yet, it's a good starting point. To summarize, there are two main branches. This is information that allows you to identify whose information it belongs to, and information that the organization has decided not to release.

items.prompt: Do you think it's okay to include any information as long as the service is safe?
items.answer: A service's policy is a service-side rule. It does not supersede any of my organization's regulations or legal obligations. Even if the service handles data safely, whether the data can be placed in an external service must be judged according to the standards set by the organization.

items.prompt: Do you think just deleting the name of the material is enough?
items.answer: In addition to name, there is contact information, account number, and other information that can be combined to determine who someone is. Which items should be deleted are specifically covered in the examples in this class.

screens.outro: I will organize the criteria I came up with by dividing them into types of information.

screens.title: Personal and confidential information
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the type of information and related policies. The final tab checks for cases where the two types overlap.

tabs.label: Personal information
tabs.body: Personal information is information that can identify a specific person. Representative examples include name, contact information, and biometric information, and also include numbers that refer to a person, such as an account number. Google's Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy prohibits the use of personal data or biometric information without legally required consent. Tracking or monitoring people without their consent is also prohibited. OpenAI's Usage Policy also does not permit attempts to gather, monitor, or profile other people's private or sensitive information without their permission.

tabs.label: confidential information
tabs.body: Confidential information is information that an organization has decided not to release. Examples include business plans, contract terms, and internal pricing policies that have not yet been made public. It differs from personal information in that it can be confidential information even if it does not identify the person. Since the scope of confidentiality is determined by your organization's regulations, not the service policy, you must check which data is confidential according to the organization's standards.

tabs.label: In case of overlap
tabs.body: The two types can overlap. Customer lists are personal information because they identify people, but they are also confidential information because organizations keep them private to protect customer relationships. So, you should not judge it to be safe based on just one criterion. We consider whether the person can be recognized and whether the organization has decided to keep it private.

tabs.label: General information
tabs.body: Data that has already been made public, statistics that do not refer to a specific person, and general knowledge are close to general information. In general, there is little burden to input, but even if it is public data, there may be copyright or usage conditions, so it is better to know the source of the data before writing.

screens.outro: After determining the type of information, let's look at what the service documentation requires of the user.

screens.title: What does the usage policy and conduct principles say?
screens.lead: Open each item one by one to see how the roles differ depending on the type of document. You can open and compare multiple items at the same time.

items.title: Usage Policy: Rules you must follow
items.body: A usage policy is a document that sets out what is allowed and what is prohibited for those who use the service. OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic each have their own policies. Anthropic's usage policy is divided into three categories: universal standards that apply to all users, requirements for high-risk use cases, and additional guidelines for specific use cases such as chatbots and agents. The privacy section prohibits sharing personal information without consent or illegally accessing private data.

items.title: Model Spec: How the model should behave
items.body: OpenAI's Model Specification is a document that describes how the model is intended to behave. It deals with the behavioral principles of the model, not rules for users to follow. The document outlines a commitment to protecting individual privacy in interactions with AI, citing not providing sensitive personal data as an example of the limitations the model must adhere to.

items.title: Claude constitution: Values pursued by the model
items.body: Anthropic's Claude constitution describes Claude's values and personality. Among these values ​​are personal privacy and freedom from undue surveillance. This document is also a principle that the model considers when making decisions, rather than a rule that users must follow.

items.title: What policies do not replace
items.body: These documents are all rules and principles of the service provider. It does not supersede my organization's security policies, contracts with customers, or legal obligations regarding privacy. Even if the use is permitted by the service, it may be prohibited by your organization, so the organization's standards must always be included in the judgment before entering.

screens.outro: Now that you know where the rules come from, let's read how the service actually handles the data entered.

screens.title: Read how the service handles data
screens.lead: Using the Gemini API abuse monitoring document as an example, follow the path the entered data takes step by step with the arrow to the right.

visual.alt: Data processing flow diagram with four steps: input, storage, review, and use restrictions.

steps.title: Step 1: Enter
steps.body: The prompts sent to the Gemini API, the accompanying contextual information, and the output generated by the model are what is processed. In other words, the material I attached also enters this flow as context information.

steps.title: Step 2: Storage
steps.body: Google says it retains prompts, context information, and output for 55 days to detect and prevent policy violations. This means that it will remain in the service for a certain period of time from the moment it is entered, so it is best not to enter information from the beginning that should not be entered.

steps.title: Step 3: Review
steps.body: Content caught in our safety filters and abuse detection systems may be reviewed by authorized Google employees. Access is limited to authorized personnel through our internal governance assessment and review management platform.

steps.title: Step 4: Limit usage
steps.body: It states that data recorded for abuse monitoring is only used to enforce policies and prevent violations, and is not used to train or fine-tune AI models other than those for policy enforcement.

steps.title: How to read
steps.body: The takeaway from this example is that each service has documented documentation of how it should be stored, reviewed, and used for learning. Before using a new service for work, I look for these three things in the documentation, read them, and check whether they match the sensitivity of my data.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the service's data processing rules, let's explain the decision process with a business example.

screens.title: Commentary: Customer data summary task
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process of creating an inputtable form for summarizing customer consultation records. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: I have 500 customer consultation records, and I want to summarize the types of complaints and write them into an improvement report. The records are a mix of customer names and contact information, account numbers, consultation details, and some undisclosed contract terms.

steps.title: Step 1: Identify your purpose
steps.body: What is needed in this summary is the type of complaint, not your name and contact information. Deciding on your purpose first will help you keep only the items you need. The strongest protection is not entering information you don't need in the first place.

steps.title: Step 2: Remove identifying information or generalize
steps.body: Erase personally identifiable items such as name, contact information, and account number. If necessary, generalize by converting it to a number like Customer A. Not only does it delete one item, but it also checks to see if there are any combinations left that would reveal who it is when multiple items are combined.

steps.title: Step 3: Exclude confidential items
steps.body: Exclude items that your organization has decided to keep private, such as undisclosed contract terms or internal pricing information, unless they are relevant to the purpose of the summary. Deleting personal information does not mean confidentiality is gone.

steps.title: Step 4: Make sure your environment is acceptable
steps.body: Check the data processing practices of the service and your organization's regulations, and only summarize in permitted circumstances. This is where I read the documentation about how long the service keeps the data and how it is used for review and learning.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: Columns from the original table are removed one by one, leaving only items such as type of complaint and time of occurrence, creating a table that can be entered. As a result, sensitive information does not reach AI while performing the same tasks.

screens.outro: Since we have looked at the pre-input process as an example, let us organize the judgment table by data type.

screens.title: Explanation: Judgment table before input
screens.lead: Each row of the table is a type of data, and the right column is a judgment and reason for that type. Read the rows and see how the conditions become stricter as the sensitivity increases.

data.caption: Input judgment table by data type
rows: It is already public and does not refer to a specific person. Just check the source to see if there are conditions for use.
You can enter after checking the regulations.
Although it has been processed so that people cannot be recognized, it must be checked that there is no risk of identification when combined.
Enter only when permission conditions and consent are confirmed.
This applies to personal information. Since use without consent may be prohibited by policy, please replace identifying information in a de-identified form whenever possible.
Enter only in services permitted by organizational regulations.
This is confidential information. Regardless of the service policy, the organization's regulations take precedence.
Contact the department in charge without entering information.
If you enter something when you are not sure, there is no going back. It takes much less time to ask.
data.notes: This table is the starting point for judgment. Because actual standards may vary depending on your organization's regulations and legal obligations, we recommend translating the table entries into your organization's terms.

screens.outro: Through the judgment table, we will summarize that confirmation before input is the strongest protection.

screens.title: Judgment before input is the strongest protection.
screens.lead: Let's organize what we've seen so far into one habit. Please read while thinking about the materials I cover. The last three confirmation questions are criteria you can use right away before entering anything, and if you memorize them, your judgment will be much faster.

paragraphs: Personal information is information that can identify a person, and confidential information is information that the organization has decided not to release. Since the two may overlap, check them separately based on each criterion.

Usage policies are service-side rules. Just because a service allows it doesn’t mean your organization allows it, and you must follow your organization’s regulations and legal obligations separately. The documentation also explains how long the service retains your data and how it is reviewed.

The most secure way to enter is to remove identifying information, leaving only the necessary information. And the strongest protection is the judgment you make before you type, not the actions you take after you type. If you are not sure, do not enter it and ask the responsible department. This practice applies equally to all input, such as translation, drafting, and tabulating, as well as summarizing material.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Check three things before entering: Does this data identify people? Has the organization decided to keep it private? Did you leave only the necessary items?

glossary.def: This is information that can identify a specific individual. This includes name, contact information, biometric information, etc.
This is information that the organization has decided not to share externally. This includes undisclosed plans, contract terms, etc.
This is a document that sets out what actions a service provider allows or prohibits from users.
It is a habit to check the type and sensitivity of data before inserting it into AI.
This involves erasing or generalizing personally identifiable items, such as names or contact information.

misconceptions.myth: They say the service is safe, so you can put in any data.
misconceptions.fact: The service's policies and my organization's regulations and legal obligations are separate. Even use permitted by the service may be prohibited by the organization, so judgment is required before entering.

misconceptions.myth: Just deleting the name is enough.
misconceptions.fact: You also need to deal with identifying items such as account numbers and contact information, as well as information that can be combined to identify who you are.

misconceptions.myth: Policy documents are for developers only.
misconceptions.fact: Users of the app are also subject to the service's terms of use and usage policy. Check what uses are prohibited before using it at work.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Although personal information and confidential information are different types, they can overlap.
Usage policies are the rules of the service and must be kept separate from organizational regulations and legal obligations.
Enter only the necessary information, removing any identifying information.
Judgment before input is the strongest protection.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the most sensitive material I handle, and how much can I put into AI?

checks.q: What most accurately describes the nature of your customer list?
options: It can be personal information that can identify a person, but it can also be confidential information protected by an organization.
Since it has not been made public, it is confidential information and not personal information.
If there is only a name, it is personal information, and if there is contact information, it is confidential information.
If the service usage policy allows, you may enter it in any case.
checks.explain: Personal and confidential information may overlap, and customer lists may represent both.

wrong.1: If it can identify a specific person, it is personal information.
wrong.2: Rather than dividing the two based on item type, the criteria are identity and the organization's non-disclosure policy.
wrong.3: The usage policy is a service-side rule and does not replace my organization's regulations and legal obligations.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what kind of information you just learned. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.q: Put the preparation steps in order before summarizing your customer service records
items: Identify the purpose: What you need is the type of complaint, not the name and contact information.
Remove or generalize identifying information such as name, contact information, or account number
Exclude confidential items such as undisclosed contract terms
Confirm the data processing and organizational provisions of the service and summarize them in acceptable circumstances
checks.explain: Decide what you need, strip out identifying information and confidentiality, and finally make sure your environment is acceptable.
checks.intro: Think of the preparation steps before inputting and arrange them in order. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match input judgments with types of data
right: Enter only when permission conditions and consent are confirmed.
Enter only in services permitted by organizational regulations.
You can enter after checking the regulations.
checks.explain: The higher the sensitivity, the stricter the input conditions. If you are not sure, do not enter it and contact the responsible department.
